At ONGC, we understand that sustainable growth is the need of the hour. That's the reason we
are working towards the time-bound target of achieving Net zero carbon emissions by 2038. We
are taking steps to ensure that as we continue to source conventional energy for the nation's
energy security, we are also, at the same time, increasingly focusing on tapping into renewable
energy sources so as to have a minimal impact on the environment. This transformation in the
energy sector is our commitment to the nation.

To make the country developed, we are now moving towards
‘Samudra Manthan’ (churning of the ocean). Taking forward our
Samudra Manthan, we want to work in a mission mode towards
ﬁnding oil reserves, gas reserves under the sea and hence India is
going to start the National Deep Water Exploration Mission.

Dear Shareholders,

Chairman’s Message

On behalf of the Board of Directors of Oil &
Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC/
the Company), it is my privilege to present
you with the Integrated Annual Report for
the financial year 2025-26 (FY’26), outlining
the Company’s performance.

were openly questioned, supply chains were
redrawn in real time, and energy became,
once again, an instrument of statecraft
rather than merely a commodity. The lesson
of the year is one this industry has learned
before and cannot afford to forget: energy
security and national security are no longer
separable.

The world did not settle in the year gone
by. If anything, the fault lines deepened.
Tariffs, sanctions and protectionism, once
dismissed as episodic disruptions, have
hardened into the everyday grammar of
global trade. Alliances long taken for granted

For the oil and gas industry, the year
carried a particular edge. Crude oil, which
had realised comfortably higher prices in
recent years, softened through much of
FY’26 as fresh supply outran demand. A
soft market is an unforgiving examiner.

Let me turn now to the year’s performance.
During FY’26, your Company produced
20.501 MMT of crude oil and 19.966 BCM
of natural gas, including our share from
joint ventures, along with 2.561 MMT
of value-added products. On paper,
maintaining production close to the
previous year’s levels may read as standing
still. It is nothing of the sort. Many of our
principal fields are mature producing
assets; Mumbai High itself has been on
production for five decades. To hold the
line against their natural decline demands
relentless intervention, through global best
practices, advanced recovery methods and
disciplined reservoir management. Your
Company drilled 501 wells during the year,
of which 100 were exploratory, and the
sheer intensity of that campaign is itself a
statement of intent.
In response to the natural decline of our
mature offshore fields, your Company has
continued to strengthen its framework
for engaging global technical expertise.
The most consequential step of the year
came on 26 December 2025, when we
placed the Notice of Award for the ONGCbp Redevelopment Phase-1 Scheme at

Natural gas will play an increasingly
central role in your Company’s growth and
in India’s journey towards a cleaner, gasbased economy. Supported by an enabling
policy environment and expanding demand,
your Company is continuing to advance
the development and monetisation of
its gas resources. A defining milestone
of the year was the commencement of
gas production in March 2026 from the
Daman Upside Development Project
(DUDP), which develops the additional
gas reserves of the Tapti-Daman block in
the Western Offshore. Your Company also
advanced the monetisation of additional
gas resources: commercial gas sales from
the North Karanpura Coal Bed Methane
block commenced on 16 May 2025, and the
Chinnewala Discovered Small Field block in
Rajasthan began production on 25 August
2025. Backed by India’s expanding city
gas distribution network and stable policy
support, your Company is well-positioned
to lead this transition.

Building on this momentum, your Company
maintained a sustained and intensive
exploration programme during FY’26.
Three new hydrocarbon discoveries were
notified in its operated offshore acreages.
In addition, testing concluded during the
year established 55 wells as hydrocarbonbearing, including wells drilled in previous
years. These outcomes reinforce the value
of persistent exploration and disciplined
follow-through across our acreages.
We acquired 957.25 LKM of 2D and
4,631.04 SKM of 3D seismic data, much
of it in our Open Acreage Licensing Policy
(OALP) blocks, where ONGC continues to
hold the country’s largest acreage position
under the OALP rounds concluded up
to Round IX. Across these blocks, your
Company has now cumulatively drilled 79
exploratory wells and made 13 discoveries,
from Amrit, Moonga and Moti in the earlier
rounds to Vajramani, MBS191HCA-1 and
MBS202HAA-1 in the year just concluded.
Your Company also drilled eight wells
targeting Basement exploration, from
East Lakhibari and Kasomarigaon in
the Assam Shelf to the Padra cluster in
the Cambay Basin, and pressed on with
high-pressure, high-temperature (HP-HT)
reservoirs. During the year, we monetised
the Gojalia-14 and Chitabari-1 discoveries
in Tripura and Anor-1 in the Cambay
Basin. Reserve accretion in 2P terms from
ONGC-operated areas in India stood at
44.01 MMTOE, a Reserve Replacement
Ratio of 1.17. For a company with a
mature producing portfolio, replacing
more reserves than we produced during
the year is a significant achievement and
an important affirmation of the enduring
potential of our domestic resource base.
The exploration story that stirs the greatest
anticipation, however, lies in deep water.
As deepwater and ultra-deepwater sectors
redraw the map of global exploration, your
Company has answered with both ambition
and technical resolve. Under PROJECT
DeepX, we have mobilised a specialist
taskforce and finalised plans to double
our deepwater drilling effort over the next
two years, in step with the Government’s
Samudra Manthan campaign. During FY’26,
your Company drilled four exploratory wells

Amidst this global turbulence, India
remained the world’s fastest-growing
major economy, with real GDP provisionally
estimated to have grown 7.7 per cent during
the year. India’s energy demand grew
alongside its economy, and it is this demand
your Company exists to serve. That single
fact shaped every major decision we made
in FY’26.

The amendment to the Oilfields (Regulation
and Development) Act, which provides fiscal
stability, resource sharing and an expeditious
dispute-resolution mechanism, is a bold and
welcome step by the Government of India to
reinvigorate exploration and production in
the country.

Annexures to the Board’s Report

Even as the energy transition gathers
pace, the world’s demand for reliable
and affordable hydrocarbons remains
undiminished. This is the dual mandate that
defines our era: to keep the nation securely
supplied with conventional energy today,
while building the low-carbon enterprise
of tomorrow. For your Company, this is
not merely a moment to manage; it is an
inflection point to lead. Our legacy will be
shaped by the courage of our choices, by
the readiness to invest beyond the current
cycle, to adopt new technologies at scale,
and to stand not as a passenger of the
transition but as one of its architects.

the long-term prospects of our Western

ONGC is implementing a comprehensive

major capital projects aimed at improving
production performance and asset integrity.
Significant investments are being made in
strengthening infrastructure, augmenting
facilities, and improving field connectivity.
This commitment is reflected in our ongoing
capital investment programme in Western
Offshore, with projects more than ` 4,00,000
million currently under implementation. As
these interventions mature, we expect their
benefits to progressively materialise from
FY 2027-28 onwards, leading to enhanced
production, improved recovery, and
sustained value creation in the years ahead.

artificial intelligence is moving from pilot
to practice across exploration, drilling,
reservoir management and corporate
functions, with several in-house solutions
already delivering measurable gains
in production, cost and downtime.

4 copyrights from Intellectual Property
India. What encourages me most is that
much of this change is driven by our own
people, through initiatives such as the
Udbhav hackathon, where employees build
the very tools they go on to use.
In terms of financial performance, your
Company’s revenue from operations stood

at ` 1,325,081 million in FY’26, against
` 1,378,463 million in FY’25, primarily
reflecting lower crude-oil realisations
during the year. Profit After Tax stood at
` 328,940 million, against ` 356,103 million
in FY’25, with the moderation attributable
mainly to the same market pressures. Yet
what the year could not diminish matters
more than what it affected. Your Company
continues to maintain a strong balance
sheet, with a Debt-Equity Ratio of just 0.02:1
and a Return on Capital Employed of 22.46
per cent. We contributed ` 558,653 million to
the national exchequer. Your Board declared
interim dividends of ` 6.00 and ` 6.25 per
share during FY’26 and has recommended
a final dividend of ` 1.00 per share, subject
to shareholder approval. The total dividend
payout for FY’26 would accordingly be
` 166,689 million, representing a payout
ratio of 51 per cent. Through cycles high
and low, rewarding the trust you place in
your Company is not negotiable.
Your Company’s ambitious ‘Net Zero by 2038’
strategy for Scope-1 and Scope-2 emissions
is not only an environmental commitment
but also an avenue for growth and value
creation, backed by a comprehensive
investment and implementation roadmap.
ONGC Green Limited (OGL), our whollyowned subsidiary, continued to scale its
renewable portfolio, which now stands at
2.853 GW, in line with the Company’s goal
of reaching 10 GW by 2030. This growth has
come through both organic and inorganic
routes, including the acquisition of OGL
One Limited and, through the ONGC NTPC
Green joint venture, Ayana Renewable
Power Private Limited. During the year,
your Company awarded a 300 MW ISTSconnected solar power project for captive
use, with the corresponding wind tender
awarded on 5th June 2026, translating
into significant power-cost savings.
Your Company’s Scope-1 and Scope-2
emissions fell 7.26 per cent during the
year to 8.81 MMTCO2e, a tangible marker
of progress on our decarbonisation journey.
Your Company is also advancing its first
Carbon Capture and Storage pilot at the
Gandhar Field, envisaging the injection of
approximately 100 tonnes of CO2 per day
into depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs. The
initiative, supported by the establishment
of a dedicated CCUS laboratory and
collaboration with leading research
institutions, marks an important step
towards developing indigenous carbonstorage capability. Natural gas, meanwhile,
will remain an important partner to
renewable power, providing flexibility and

reliability as the energy system transitions
towards lower-carbon sources.
Your Company’s subsidiaries and joint
ventures serve as a strategic buffer against
the inherent volatility of the exploration
and production business. Through their
diversified operations spanning the
upstream, midstream and downstream
segments, they fortify the ONGC Group’s
resilience to sectoral fluctuations and
cement ONGC’s position as India’s
leading integrated energy enterprise. On
a consolidated basis, the ONGC Group
delivered a resilient performance in FY’26,
anchored by HPCL’s highest-ever combined
refining throughput of 26.04 MMT and a
group capital expenditure of ` 611,308
million deployed across the value chain.
ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL), the whollyowned overseas arm of your Company,
holds participating interests in 29 oil and gas
projects across 14 countries, comprising
14 producing, 5 discovered or underdevelopment, 7 exploration and 3 pipeline
projects. Production from overseas assets
during FY’26 was 9.671 MMTOE, comprising
6.908 MMT of crude oil and 2.763 BCM of
natural gas. During the year, OVL crossed
a historic milestone, reaching a cumulative
total of 224.32 MMTOE of hydrocarbon
production. A landmark development was
the lifting of Force Majeure on the Area-1
Mozambique LNG project in November
2025, enabling the full-scale resumption
of project execution, with first LNG now
targeted for July 2028. Following sustained
engagement with Ministry of Energy of
the Russian Federation, ONGC Videsh
successfully formalized the acquisition of
its 20% equity stake in Sakhalin-1 LLC on
5th December 2025. This marked a significant
milestone in securing the continuity of
ONGC Videsh’s strategic investment in one
of Russia’s premier upstream oil and gas
projects, despite a challenging geopolitical
and sanctions environment. In another
recent development, OVL has been granted
Specific License by the U.S. Office of Foreign
Assets Control (OFAC), enabling continued
operations, investments, and marketing
of production from its Venezuelan assets,
including SCB and PCB. It also permits
the acquisition of additional participating
interests and new oil and gas opportunities
in Venezuela thereby strengthening OVL’s
international operations and growth
prospects.
In the downstream segment, your Company
continued to benefit from the strong
performance of its key subsidiaries.

During the year, your Company also formed
Bharat Ethane One IFSC Private Limited
and Bharat Ethane Two IFSC Private

O.S.K. Lines, Japan, to secure the longterm transportation of ethane for OPaL.

the vessels scheduled for delivery during
FY 2028–29, the initiative marks an
important step towards strengthening
feedstock security, building specialised
energy-logistics capability and supporting
the long-term competitiveness of OPaL.

ONGC Petro additions Limited (OPaL), now

restructuring, including the additional

EBITDA recorded a significant turnaround,

strengthen value capture across the chain,
your Company is progressing the formation
of a dedicated petrochemical trading joint
venture with MRPL and OPaL, subject to the
requisite governmental approval.

drills were conducted during the year to
strengthen emergency preparedness and
response capabilities. Aligned with the
Mission LiFE initiative and the ‘Ek Ped

environmental commitment. Safety, at

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26

Arun Kumar Singh
Chairman and CEO
Mr. Arun Kumar Singh is the Chairman and CEO of ONGC and the ONGC Group of Companies. He
assumed this role on December 7, 2022. Mr. Singh additionally serves as the Chairman of ONGC
Videsh Limited (OVL), Mangalore Reﬁnery & Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL), ONGC Petro
additions Limited (OPaL), ONGC Green Ltd. (OGL) and ONGC Energy Centre Trust (OECT). The
ONGC Group is having dominance in the E&P sector in India and has a signiﬁcant presence abroad
through its 100% subsidiary OVL. The group also has notable interests in reﬁning, petrochemicals,
power and renewables. Mr Singh is also on the Board of Petronet LNG Ltd. (PLL).
An industry stalwart, Mr. Singh commands nearly four decades of extensive experience in the Oil &
Gas industry. He is a Gold Medalist in Mechanical Engineering from the National Institute of
Technology, Patna.
Previously, Mr. Singh served as the Chairman and Managing Director of Bharat Petroleum
Corporation Limited (BPCL), a 'Maharatna' and Fortune Global 500 Company. He also chaired
Indraprastha Gas Ltd. (IGL), a Joint Venture City Gas Distribution (CGD) Company listed on Indian
Stock Exchanges. He has also held the position of President (Africa & Australia) at Bharat
PetroResources Ltd (BPRL), a BPCL subsidiary focused on oil and gas exploration, primarily
overseas.
Mr. Arun Kumar Singh is a member of Oil Industry Development Board. He is the Chairman of the
Federation of Indian Petroleum Industry's (FIPI) Governing Council and is chairing the CII Public
Sector Enterprises Council.

Before assuming his current role as Director (T&FS) of the Company, Mr.

Om Prakash Sinha
Director (Exploration)

Mr. Om Prakash Sinha is a Petroleum Engineering graduate from ISM
Dhanbad with more than 38 years of experience in ONGC in various facets
of E&P activities. He has worked in Exploration, Field Development and
Reservoir Management domains in various capacities. He has excelled in
many aspects of Reservoir Engineering, from Seismic to Simulation,
conceptualizing and execution of ﬁeld development schemes, formulation
of long term plans. He has also been instrumental in reservoir management of onshore and offshore ﬁelds, formulation of IOR schemes,
screening/implementation of EOR processes and reservoir simulation
studies. He served as the Chief of Institute of Reservoir Studies, an inhouse Institute of ONGC at Ahmedabad, dedicated for designing IOR/EOR
programmes for ﬁelds of ONGC, where he pursued the expansion of EOR
application for production enhancement in ONGC Fields. In present
changing energy-mix scenario he has also played pivotal role in conceptualizing projects on Carbon Capture Utilization and Storage (CCUS/CCS) for
carbon emission abatement to meet Net-Zero targets. He is also member
of professional bodies like SPE and SPG.
Mr. O.P. Sinha is the Chairman of ONGC Teri Biotech Limited, a joint
venture of the Company.

Mr. Satyan Kumar is an Electrical Engineering graduate from Dayalbagh
Educational Institution, Agra, he holds a Post Graduate Diploma in
Management from MDI Gurgaon and has undergone advanced leadership
training at ESCP-EAP, France.
With over 36 years of experience across the oil and gas value chain, his
career spans upstream operations, engineering, project management,
marketing, business development, petrochemicals, corporate strategy
and renewable energy, he has played a key role in shaping ONGC's longterm strategic roadmap, including diversiﬁcation into petrochemicals,
LNG and green energy, and has been associated with initiatives in solar,
wind, biofuels and other sustainable energy domains. His leadership
assignments included Executive Director – Chief Corporate Strategy,
senior roles in Engineering Services, and project leadership for critical
infrastructure and business development initiatives such as captive power
plants, the Hazira–Dahej naphtha pipeline and ONGC's ﬁrst 15 MW utilityscale solar project.

Standalone Performance at a Glance

Capital Employed = Net Working Capital + Current maturities of non-current borrowings + Net Non Current Assets excluding Capital work in
progress, intangible Oil & Gas asset in progress & capital advances, Exploratory/Developments wells & Investments

2.

Profit Margin (%) = Profit after tax for the year/Turnover

3.

Working Capital = Current Assets (Excluding Investment) - Current Liablities

4.

ROCE = Profit Before Interest, Dividend Income & Tax (PBIT excluding Dividend income) / Capital Employed

5.

Current Ratio = Current Assets (Including Current Investment) / Current Liabilities

6.

Debt Equity Ratio = Total Debt (Non-current & current) / Equity (Net Worth)

7.

Net Profit to Equity (%) = Profit after tax for the year / Equity (Net Worth)

8.

Debtor Turnover Ratio (days) = (Average Receivables/Revenue from Operations)*365

9.

Earning per share = Profit after Tax attributable to Owners of the Company / No. of Equity Shares

10.

Book value per share = Equity (Net Worth) / No. of Equity Shares

Section 1: About the Report

Reporting Period

Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited, together with its
Group Companies (collectively referred to as “ONGC” or “the
Company”), presents its Integrated Report for FY 2025-26. The
Report provides a consolidated view of ONGC’s financial and nonfinancial performance, reflecting its commitment to transparency,
accountability, and sustainable value creation for stakeholders.

The disclosures in this report cover the Company’s performance
for the financial year 1st April 2025 to 31st March 2026.

Reporting Principles
This Integrated Report serves as an annual disclosure prepared
in accordance with the principles of the International Integrated
Reporting <IR> Framework issued by the International Integrated
Reporting Council (IIRC), focusing on value creation over the
short, medium, and long term.
The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards 2021, including:
GRI 1: Foundation 2021; GRI 2: General Disclosures 2021; GRI 3:
Material Topics 2021; GRI 11: Oil and Gas Sector Standard (2021).
The Report also demonstrates ONGC’s contribution towards the
United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with
relevant SDGs mapped across key disclosures. Additionally,
the Report complies with applicable statutory and regulatory
requirements, including:
•

The Companies Act, 2013 and related rules

•

Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Listing
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR)
Regulations, 2015

Value Creation Approach
Aligned with the Framework, ONGC presents its strategy and
performance through the lens of six capitals, demonstrating how
the Company creates, preserves, and transforms value:
•

Financial Capital: Financial performance,
deployment, and returns to investors

capital

•

Manufactured Capital: Physical assets, infrastructure, and
operational capabilities

•

Human Capital: Workforce development, health and safety,
and employee engagement

•

Intellectual Capital: Innovation, research and development,
and technology capabilities

•

Social and Relationship Capital: Stakeholder engagement,
partnerships, and community development

•

Natural Capital: Environmental stewardship, including
emissions management, resource efficiency, and climate
action

performance of ONGC and selected Group entities.

This includes gathering input through formal surveys, collecting

help the Company identify key concerns and respond effectively
in ways that support its operations and strengthen stakeholder

Embedding Stakeholder Perspectives in Business Decisions
Stakeholder inputs gathered across ONGC’s business units are systematically reviewed and prioritized before being integrated into
the Company’s business planning processes to ensure alignment with strategic objectives. At the corporate level, these insights
are evaluated by the senior management to enable informed oversight and decision-making. In addition, findings from the annual
stakeholder engagement survey are analyzed to assess current performance and inform the identification of priority focus areas for the
upcoming year.

Double Materiality Assessment
GRI 3-1, 3-2, 3-3
Following the successful completion and implementation
of double materiality assessment in FY 2024-25, ONGC has
continued to strengthen and institutionalize this approach in FY
2025-26 as part of its larger sustainability governance framework.
This progression reflects the organization’s efforts to keep pace
with evolving global ESG reporting expectations.
The double materiality assessment framework enables ONGC to
systematically identify, evaluate, and prioritize key sustainability
topics that significantly impact the environment, society, and the
organization’s financial performance. The process considers both
actual and potential impacts, encompassing positive and negative
dimensions across financial and non-financial parameters
throughout ONGC’s operations and value chain.
The materiality assessment is reviewed annually and updated
periodically to ensure it remains responsive to evolving
stakeholder expectations, regulatory developments, and changes
in the business and risk environment. This structured review
process helps determine whether updates to the methodology or
a comprehensive reassessment of material topics are required.
To further strengthen its robustness, ONGC has embedded the
materiality assessment within its Enterprise Risk Management
(ERM) framework. This integration enables a holistic evaluation
of how internal and external factors influence sustainability
priorities while enhancing the organization’s ability to anticipate
and respond to emerging risks. The process is supported by
a detailed contextual analysis and impact mapping exercise,
leveraging a wide range of internal and external inputs. These

include corporate strategy documents, applicable regulations
and policies, enterprise risk registers, stakeholder feedback, and
secondary research sources such as media coverage, investor
insights, grievance redressal records, social media trends, and
third-party ESG ratings assessments.
In addition, ONGC continues to benchmark its approach against
globally recognized frameworks and industry best practices.
Reference points include publications such as the World
Economic Forum’s Global Risk Report, Sustainability Accounting
Standards Board (SASB) standards, and the MSCI ESG Industry
Materiality Map, ensuring continuous improvement in identifying
and managing material sustainability issues.
The Concept of Double Materiality
Impact Materiality
(Inside-out perspective)
The extent to which ONGC's business activities may have
a positive or negative Impact on the environment & society
Society and
Environmental

Business
Financial Materiality
(Outside-in perspective)

The extent to which external sustainability-related factors
positively or negatively Impact ONGC's cash ﬂows, performance,
cost of capital or access to ﬁnance of the business

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26

31

Overview

INDUSTRIAL
ASSOCIATIONS

Annexures to the Board’s Report

P Regulatory Compliance

Double Materiality Assessment Process
ONGC identified a set of sustainability issues that affect the economy, environment, and people across its operations and business
relationships, guided by the European Sustainability Disclosure Standards and mapped across key stages of the value chain. In FY 2024–
25, the Company conducted a comprehensive review of its material topics to reflect evolving stakeholder priorities, emerging regulatory
requirements, recent business developments, and the adoption of a double materiality approach. This review led to a reassessment of
the relative significance of certain issues.
The Company follows an ongoing approach to engage both internal and external stakeholders. Insights from these interactions were
used to assess impact along with financial materiality, which then guided the development of ESG goals and targets based on their level
of importance. The assessment process has been validated by an independent third-party assurance provider.
Overview of Assessment Methodology
Deﬁning the Sustainability
Landscape
Identiﬁcation of pool of
material topics
A broad universe of
sustainability issues was
identiﬁed using globally
recognized frameworks and
peer benchmarking in
alignment with ESRS.
This process was further
informed by ESG initiatives,
Oil & Gas industry trends and
media analysis, distilling to a
list of 28 key material topics.

Identiﬁcation of Impacts,
Risks & Opportunities (IROS)
Impact Identiﬁcation
Environmental and social

Biodiversity

GRI 11.4, 101-1, 101-2, 101-4, 101-5, 101-7

CAPITALS
IMPACTED

SDGs ALIGNED

VALUE CHAIN IMPACT BOUNDARY
Upstream

Own Operations

Downstream

ONGC's operations, including land acquisition, site
development, and onshore and offshore drilling, have the
potential to signiﬁcantly affect biodiversity and surrounding
ecosystems. These activities may contribute to habitat
fragmentation, loss of vegetation cover, and disturbance to
both terrestrial and marine species.
In addition, noise generated during exploration and drilling
can interfere with wildlife behavior, leading to disorientation
and disruption of natural communication patterns. Many
species depend on sound for navigation, mating, and locating
food, and prolonged exposure to high noise levels can impair
these functions.
Ultimately, such disturbances may affect their survival and
reproductive success inﬂuencing the balance and resilience
of local ecosystems.

FINANCIAL
MATERIALITY

IMPACT
MATERIALITY

Risk

Actual
Negative Impact

TIME HORIZON MAPPING
Short Term

Medium Term

Long Term

Approach for Risk Mitigation
ONGC follows a structured approach towards biodiversity
conservation and ecological restoration. Environmental
Impact Assessments (EIAs) are carried out prior to the
commencement of projects to evaluate potential impacts
and deﬁne mitigation measures. Under its Environmental
Management Plan, dedicated resources are assigned for
biodiversity protection, along with the implementation of
targeted conservation actions.
These plans are submitted to the State Wildlife Division and
require approval from the Ministry of Environment, Forest
and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) before operations begin.
Key measures include habitat restoration, land reclamation,
and rehabilitation of impacted ecosystems, which are
undertaken across different stages of the project lifecycle to
support long-term ecological stability.

5 hectares of land
As part of the Eco-restoration Project under the Green Credit Program (GCP) is currently under implementation
and monitoring stage in Goa in FY 2025-26

Downstream

ONGC operates in a complex risk environment where
challenges can emerge from multiple sources, including
market ﬂuctuations, geopolitical developments, legal
exposures, technological breakdowns, and environmental
events.
Within this context, maintaining asset integrity remains
critical, as it supports the effective management of asset
performance and degradation over their entire lifecycle,
from design and installation to operation and eventual
decommissioning, while safeguarding ﬁnancial stability and
operational continuity.

Short Term

Medium Term

Long Term

Approach for Risk Mitigation
ONGC has established an integrated risk management
framework, which includes:
• A structured asset integrity management system
designed to ensure that all physical assets are subject to
regular inspection, evaluation, and maintenance so they
continue to operate safely and reliably
• Compliance with established national and international
standards, including ISO 55000 and guidelines issued by
OISD
• Detailed emergency response and crisis management
protocols to address incidents such as oil spills, gas leaks,
and ﬁres. These frameworks are periodically reviewed
and updated to remain aligned with evolving risk
scenarios and operational changes
• Independent third-party audits and certiﬁcation surveys
are conducted for offshore structures, while corrective
actions are being implemented for the remaining assets
to ensure continued structural integrity, operational
reliability, and safety
• Ongoing training and capability-building initiatives aimed
at strengthening workforce preparedness to manage
critical incidents and uphold asset integrity across all
operational areas

substantial quantities of both hazardous and non-hazardous
waste generated during exploration, drilling, and production
activities. This includes drilling muds, sludges, and chemical

Evolving Global Dynamics: Uncertain Returns from Low-Carbon Investments
As ONGC expands its presence in renewable energy and emerging low-carbon technologies, the Company is exposed to evolving risks
linked to fluctuations in technology costs, policy support mechanisms, and market dynamics. Investments in areas such as solar, wind,
hydrogen, biofuels, and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS), along with acquisitions and joint ventures, may face uncertainties
in achieving projected returns or may involve extended payback periods compared to initial expectations.
ONGC’s Strategy in Mitigation
To navigate these uncertainties, ONGC adopts a rigorous evaluation approach for all low-carbon investments. Each opportunity
undergoes detailed financial analysis, scenario-based stress testing, and comprehensive due diligence to assess viability and optimize
investment decisions.
In addition, periodic portfolio reviews are conducted to track performance against projected outcomes. This enables timely corrective

During FY 2025-26, ONGC continued to strengthen its asset base
through focused exploration and development activities. The
Company drilled four exploration wells in the ultra-deep waters
of the Andaman Basin and acquired 508 LKM of 2D and 3,377 SKM
of 3D seismic data in the Mahanadi Basin, enhancing subsurface
understanding and exploration capability. Drilling of the first
stratigraphic well (AND-P-1) in the Andaman ultra-deep waters
is also underway under a Government of India initiative.

Further, in line with its strategy to unlock potential in lesserexplored areas, ONGC drilled 13 exploratory wells across CategoryII and III basins, covering Andaman UDW, Bengal Onland, Kutch
Onland, and other basins. During the year, the Company reported
three hydrocarbon discoveries in Mumbai Offshore (shallow
waters), including two new prospects and one new pool. Notably,
the MBS191HCA-1 well established a new gas discovery in the
Chinchini Formation, adding to ONGC’s resource base.

Advancing Enhanced Oil Recovery through Advanced Technology
ONGC strengthened its production capabilities with the commissioning of its Alkaline-Surfactant-Polymer (ASP) plant at the Jhalora
field in June 2025, marking a major milestone in enhanced oil recovery.
The plant, ONGC’s largest with a capacity of 2,100 m³/day is designed to deliver incremental oil production of 0.598 MMT by FY
2039–40, translating to an additional recovery of 4.27% from the reservoir.

Inauguration of ASP-Jhalora by Director (Production) Pankaj Kumar

Developed under a ` 534.3 million contract, the project incorporates advanced automation, real-time monitoring, and efficient
chemical injection processes across 14 injection and 26 producing wells, enhancing operational efficiency and recovery performance.
The initiative also integrates sustainability measures, including the use of treated effluent water and elimination of diesel-powered
systems, aligning with ONGC’s long-term environmental goals while maximising resource recovery from mature fields.
The commissioning of ASP Jhalora Plant reinforces ONGC Ahmedabad Asset’s position at the forefront of innovation and operational
excellence, setting new benchmarks in project execution and hydrocarbon management.
The Company continues to strengthen its manufactured capital
through ongoing enhancement of existing assets and the
development of new infrastructure, supported by strategic
collaborations and digital transformation initiatives. ONGC
entered a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Indian Oil on
27th January 2026 to explore avenues for technical collaboration
and participation in upcoming exploration bid rounds. The
agreement reflects a shared intent to build operational synergies
and leverage combined expertise across the exploration value
chain. By fostering collaboration between the two PSUs, the
initiative is expected to contribute to more efficient deployment of
resources and capabilities.

Our Journey Toward a Cleaner Energy Mix
ONGC has expanded its presence in specialized energy logistics
through the formation of two joint venture companies with Mitsui
O.S.K. Lines (MOL), Japan for the transportation of ethane to
OPaL. These entities are registered at GIFT City, Gandhinagar,
with the associated vessels being Indian-flagged, supporting
domestic capability in strategic energy transportation.
ONGC awarded a 300 MW ISTS-connected solar power project in
November 2025 for captive consumption, with a corresponding
wind project under process. The initiative is expected to support
compliance with Renewable Consumption Obligations (RCO)
while enabling significant savings in power costs.

Strengthening Green Energy Capabilities through Strategic Collaboration
ONGC Green Limited signed a Memorandum of Understanding with IIM Nagpur to advance research, policy development, and
capacity building in renewable and emerging energy domains. The collaboration supports ONGC’s long-term vision of building a
sustainable and resilient energy ecosystem.
The partnership focuses on key areas such as energy storage, biofuels, green hydrogen, carbon markets, and ESG frameworks,
while also enabling leadership development and policy insights. It is expected to strengthen ONGC’s growing renewable portfolio and
accelerate the integration of future-ready energy solutions.
Technology-Led Efficiency Enhancement at Hazira Plant
ONGC’s Hazira Plant commissioned a Hydrodynamic Cavitation
(HyCa)-based treatment reactor as part of its new technology
induction initiative. Installed in Cooling Tower Phase III-A, the
pilot demonstrates the adoption of advanced process technology
to enhance operational efficiency. The system enables improved
treatment performance with reduced chemical usage, optimizes
resource consumption, and lowers energy requirements for
pumping, resulting in cost efficiencies and improved plant
performance.

Environmental Stewardship and Resource Use
In line with its Vision 2040 and commitment to sustainable
development, ONGC places strong emphasis on environmental
stewardship within its strategic and operational framework.
As India’s leading upstream oil and gas Company, ONGC
acknowledges its responsibility to utilize natural resources
efficiently while minimizing the environmental footprint of its
exploration and production activities. The Organization follows
a forward-looking approach that focuses on improving energy
efficiency,

reducing

emissions,

controlling

pollution,

and

optimizing the use of natural resources across its operations.

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26

57

Overview

Natural capital remains integral to ONGC’s operations, and
its responsible management continues to be essential for
environmental sustainability and long-term resilience. With
climate change emerging as a critical global concern, ONGC
recognizes the importance of managing natural resources
efficiently to reduce environmental impact and support mitigation
efforts. As a responsible Organization, we are committed to
protecting biodiversity, preserving ecosystems, and adopting
cleaner and more resource-efficient technologies across its
operations. In FY 2025–26, the Organization has continued to
strengthen its initiatives in areas such as water stewardship,
afforestation, waste reduction, and restoration of operational
sites, while further advancing its climate-related strategies in
line with the transition to a lower-carbon economy.

Air Pollution and Drilling impacts
Beyond greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, ONGC also maintains
a detailed inventory of key air pollutants such as sulphur oxides
(SOx), nitrogen oxides (NOx), and particulate matter (PM),
which largely arise from its exploration, drilling, and production
activities.
The development of this inventory is aligned with the same
methodological framework used for GHG accounting. It follows
a source-wise approach within the operational control boundary,
with data captured through a centralized Environmental
Performance Monitoring System across major sites, including
Uran, Dahej, and Hazira.
Emission levels are determined by tracking flue gas flow rates
and pollutant concentrations, allowing for precise estimation of
daily emissions. In addition, select facilities are equipped with
Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Systems (CAAQMS),
enabling real-time monitoring and ensuring compliance with
applicable environmental standards.

Water Management
(GRI 303-1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

Water plays a vital role in ONGC’s operations, particularly in
activities such as exploration, drilling, and production, which
require significant water usage. In view of increasing water stress
and the shared nature of this resource, ONGC has adopted a
structured approach to water stewardship. The Company aligns its
water management practices with national initiatives, including
the Jal Shakti Mission, and focuses on reducing consumption,

Across its operational assets, ONGC follows a systematic approach
to water management, with emphasis on optimizing withdrawal,
promoting reuse, and ensuring environmentally safe discharge.
Currently the Company operates 42 Effluent Treatment Plants
(ETPs) to treat significant volumes of process water generated during
exploration and production activities. These treatment systems
enable the reuse of water for operational purposes such as drilling
and reservoir pressure maintenance, thereby reducing dependence
on freshwater resources and limiting environmental impact.

ONGC commissioned an Advanced Effluent Water Treatment
Plant (AEWTP) at the Mehsana Asset with a processing

AEWTP installed at North Santhal, Mehsana Asset

Recognizing the increasing pressure on freshwater resources,
ONGC places special focus on responsible water management
in water-stressed regions, particularly in parts of western and
southern India. These areas, identified based on assessments by
the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) and internal analyses,
include several operational sites where water availability is
limited and demand may vary seasonally. In such regions,
ONGC implements stringent controls on water withdrawal and
consumption, supported by location-specific strategies aimed at
reducing dependence on freshwater and improving overall water
efficiency.
ONGC’s subsidiaries and joint ventures continue to contribute to
sustainability through targeted and innovative water management
practices. Complementing these efforts, OTPC has implemented
a rainwater harvesting system within its plant premises with a
water conservation capacity of approximately 1.78 million litres
per annum.
In FY 2025–26, OPaL further strengthened its commitment to
sustainable water management by achieving a water recycling
and reuse rate of 80.80%, equivalent to approximately 2 billion
litres of water. The Company continued to optimize cooling
water recirculation by increasing the Cycles of Concentration
(COC) in cooling towers, thereby reducing blowdown volumes
and minimizing freshwater make-up requirements. To enhance
long-term water security, OPaL also continued its participation in

the 100 MLD Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC)
desalination plant as a beneficiary, with a dedicated booking of
15 MLD of raw water. This desalination facility serves as OPaL’s
third independent source of raw water, complementing supplies
from the Narmada River and Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Ltd.
(SSNNL), reinforcing the Company’s resilience and commitment
to responsible water stewardship.
MRPL has implemented a range of water management initiatives
to reduce freshwater consumption and enhance reuse. These
include the utilization of treated municipal sewage water for
cooling tower make-up, operation of a 40 MLD desalination
plant to ensure water availability during scarcity, and advanced
wastewater treatment systems (SBR, MBR, RO) to maximize
recycling. Additionally, stripped sour water is reused in crude
desalting, while condensate recovery units and optimized cooling
water treatment further improve reuse efficiency. The use of
hydrogen peroxide in wastewater treatment also ensures highquality treated water, supporting sustainable water management
practices.
While ONGC continues to pursue enhanced wastewater recovery
and reuse across its operations, scaling up to a full Zero
Liquid Discharge (ZLD) system remains challenging due to the
generation of large volumes of solid waste and limited availability
of sustainable disposal options.

Waste Handling
(GRI 306-1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

ONGC follows a comprehensive waste management framework
across its operations to ensure safe handling, treatment,
and disposal of both hazardous and non-hazardous waste, in

compliance with applicable environmental regulations. Major
waste streams, including oily sludge, chemical sludge from ETPs,
used oil, and contaminated containers, are managed through
established procedures and authorized channels.

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26

63

The Company has also put in place a dedicated e-waste
management policy, which ensures the responsible disposal of
outdated electronic equipment and accessories through certified
recyclers and authorized take-back mechanisms. In addition,
ONGC continues to address oil-contaminated soil, one of its key
hazardous waste streams, through bioremediation processes
implemented across major asset locations such as Ahmedabad,
Mehsana, Ankleshwar, Assam, Cauvery, and Rajahmundry.
All hazardous and non-hazardous waste streams are managed
in full compliance with applicable environmental regulations.
ONGC ensures that waste is transferred exclusively to authorized
recyclers and disposal facilities approved by the Central Pollution

Control Board (CPCB) or the respective State Pollution Control
Boards (SPCBs). These certified agencies provide formal
documentation confirming safe treatment, recycling, or disposal,
thereby maintaining traceability and ensuring environmental
compliance.
In FY 2025–26, total waste recovery through recycling, reuse, and
other recovery operations increased to 195.05 MT from 116.86 MT
in FY 2024–25, while waste managed through approved disposal
methods rose by 41.3% to 9,536.08 MT, reflecting strengthened
waste management practices, improved resource recovery, and
continued regulatory compliance.

Climate Strategy, Net Zero and Carbon Management
Strategy
ONGC’s approach to climate responsibility is increasingly being
shaped by the need to integrate sustainability into core business
decisions, rather than treating it as a parallel agenda.
Within its upstream operations, ONGC is progressively
strengthening systems to track, manage, and reduce
environmental impact, with a focus on both direct and indirect
greenhouse gas emissions. Efforts are also directed towards
limiting flaring and controlling air pollutants that may affect
surrounding ecosystems and communities. This approach
reflects an ongoing effort to align operational continuity with
environmental considerations, while continuing to support the
country’s energy requirements.

ONGC operates across several ecologically sensitive areas,
including regions near national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, CRZs,
and biodiversity-rich habitats. Major operational assets such as
Jorhat, the Assam-Arakan Basin, Eastern Offshore Asset, and
the Cauvery Asset are located within or in proximity to these
environmentally significant zones.
In line with applicable regulations, including the Forest
(Conservation) Act, 1980; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986;
and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, ONGC undertakes EIAs
prior to the commencement of any project activities. The findings
from these assessments inform the development of Biodiversity
Management Plans, which are subsequently reviewed and
approved by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change (MoEF&CC) and the concerned State Wildlife Authorities.
ONGC integrates ecological restoration into its operational
approach wherever feasible. This includes activities such as land
reclamation, re-vegetation of impacted areas, and compensatory
afforestation carried out in collaboration with State Forest
Departments. The Company also developed over 78 acres of
Green Belt inside OTPC Plant premises. In coastal regions
governed by Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) provisions, the
Company undertakes measures such as mangrove restoration
and shoreline stabilization to address erosion and support
marine ecosystems. These interventions are incorporated into
Environment Management Plans (EMPs) and implemented
throughout the project lifecycle.
Some ONGC operational areas are situated in proximity to habitats
that support species listed under the IUCN Red List and Schedule I
of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Although project activities are
not expected to directly affect these species, their presence in the
surrounding ecosystem requires a precautionary and risk-aware
approach. ONGC works closely with State Wildlife Authorities to
assess potential impacts and implement appropriate safeguards,
including ecological controls and regular monitoring along with
conducting an Environmental Impact in December, 2025. These
measures reflect the Company’s commitment to responsible
operations and the long-term conservation of biodiversity within
its areas of influence.

ONGC considers biodiversity conservation an essential element
of its environmental stewardship framework. This commitment
is supported by a dedicated Biodiversity Policy that is applicable
across all domestic operations and extends to employees,
contractors, suppliers, and business partners. The policy ensures
that biodiversity considerations are embedded across the entire
project lifecycle, from exploration and operations to site closure.
It emphasizes compliance with relevant biodiversity regulations,
application of the mitigation hierarchy avoid, minimize, restore,
and offset—and the development of site-specific Biodiversity
Management Plans (BMPs). Implementation is overseen through
structured governance mechanisms under the Health, Safety
and Environment (HSE) function, with strategic direction and
monitoring provided by the Board-level HSE Committee.

Centralized, Real-Time Operations:
The establishment of the Real Time Drilling Operations Centre (RTDOC) at IDWE, Dehradun enabled centralized monitoring
of drilling and work-over activities. Supported by predictive analytics and expert inputs, RTDOC improved decision-making,
reduced operational complexity, and minimized the need for multiple monitoring systems.
•

Digitized & Efficient Well Planning:
The Digital Well Program (DWP) streamlined well planning by automating manual tasks, standardizing workflows, and
integrating planning, design, and execution on a single platform. This led to faster planning cycles, improved data consistency,
and stronger collaboration across teams.

•

Advanced Training & Capability Building:
The commissioning of the DrillSim 6000 simulator provided a highly immersive training environment with realistic rig
simulations and 3D visualization. It enhanced workforce preparedness by enabling hands-on training in complex drilling
scenarios.

•

Breakthrough in Automation:
A landmark achievement was the successful autonomous downhole steering demonstration from RTDOC for an exploratory
well in Mehsana. This pilot validated fully automated drilling, improved directional accuracy, and demonstrated the potential
of remote, data-driven operations.

Overall Impact:
These initiatives collectively strengthened ONGC’s digital capabilities, improved operational efficiency, enhanced workforce skills,
and marked a significant step toward intelligent and automated drilling operations.

Patents, Proprietary Technologies, and Digitalization
ONGC’s intellectual property portfolio is managed by the Centralized Intellectual Property Cell, which serves as the central body for
evaluating innovations across the Organization and supporting approvals, filings, and coordination with empanelled legal firms. As of FY
2025- 26, the Company has filed 17 patent applications, of which 10 have been granted. In addition, 6 copyright applications have been
filed, with 4 successfully granted.

Grievance Redressal
To promote a responsive and equitable workplace environment,
ONGC has instituted a range of formal systems to address
employee concerns and strengthen Organizational governance.
These include the Grievance Management System (GMS),
alongside Safety Committees, Internal Complaints Committees,
and a Whistle-blower mechanism.
Designed for all regular employees, the GMS functions as a
dedicated platform to address issues related to compensation,
career progression, leave, role allocation, and workplace
conditions. It follows a tiered, multi-channel process that enables
issues to be raised, reviewed, and resolved in a timely manner.
By embedding these mechanisms into its operational framework,
ONGC enhances transparency and trust within the Organization,
while fostering a fair and supportive work environment that
contributes to overall efficiency and performance.

ONGC remains committed to fostering an inclusive and accessible
workplace for Divyangjan (persons with disabilities) through a
comprehensive framework of policies, benefits, and support
measures. During this year, the Company introduced its Equal
Opportunity Policy in 2023, aligned with the Rights of Persons
with Disabilities Act, 2016, formalizing its approach towards
creating an accessible and inclusive work environment. Persons
with disabilities currently represent over 2% of ONGC’s workforce,
reflecting continued progress towards building a more diverse
and accessible Organization. The Company’s Equal Opportunity
Policy ensures a discrimination-free work environment, accessible
infrastructure, dedicated grievance redressal mechanisms, and
support for career development. Employees with disabilities are

and participation in relevant conferences and training programs,

initiatives reinforce ONGC’s commitment to inclusion, accessibility,

As part of its efforts to strengthen accountability and stakeholder
accessibility, ONGC established a dedicated online Grievance
Redressal Portal (https://grievance.ongc.co.in/), creating a
streamlined digital interface for lodging and tracking concerns.
Developed in alignment with the Digital India initiative, the
platform is aimed at improving transparency and enabling
more effective engagement between the Organization and its
stakeholders.

users, including citizens, vendors, current employees, and former
employees, allowing them to raise issues connected to any
operational unit of ONGC in a structured and accessible manner.
During FY 2025–26, the Company recorded 5 instances of sexual
harassment and 3 cases pertaining to workplace discrimination.
The discrimination-related matters were reviewed by the Internal
Redressal Grievance Committee (IRGC), which includes five
members with representation from the SC community. Following
detailed examination, the Committee concluded that the cases
were linked to Performance Appraisal Rating (PAR) assessments
and did not constitute discrimination, with necessary actions
taken thereafter.

Human Rights
ONGC integrates respect for human rights into its business
conduct and value chain, recognizing it as a core element of
responsible and sustainable operations. As a founding member
of the Global Compact Network India (GCNI), the Company
aligns its approach with the ten principles of the UN Global
Compact, covering areas such as human rights, labor practices,
environmental stewardship, and ethical business conduct.

ONGC supports this commitment through established systems
and oversight mechanisms designed to address concerns and
ensure compliance. These include digital grievance redressal
platforms, structured safety forums, Internal Complaints
Committees under POSH provisions, and a formal whistle-blower
and vigilance framework. Together, these mechanisms help
uphold standards related to workplace safety, fair labor practices,
non-discrimination, freedom of association, and ethical conduct.
Oversight is further strengthened through an independent Chief
Vigilance Officer reporting to the Central Vigilance Commission,
reinforcing accountability and governance discipline across the
Organization.

located in Khola village, which serves students from remote
and economically weaker backgrounds, by providing a school
bus under its CSR initiative. The intervention was undertaken in
response to a requirement for transportation support, as many
students faced challenges in accessing the school regularly due
to distance and limited connectivity.
The provision of safe and reliable transport has helped improve
student attendance and ease the daily commute, particularly for
those residing in remote parts of the village. By addressing a key
access barrier, the initiative supports continuity in education and
contributes to creating a more enabling learning environment. It
also reflects ONGC’s continued focus on strengthening grassroots
educational infrastructure and improving access to opportunities
for underserved communities.
ONGC’s Eastern Offshore Asset, Kakinada, supported inclusive
education by providing a 36-seater bus to a special aid school for
children with disabilities. The initiative improves safe and reliable
transportation, helping reduce absenteeism and enabling better
access to education and care.

Acquisition,

ONGC follows a structured process for land acquisition based
on operational needs, using both temporary and permanent
arrangements. Temporary land use is managed through lease
or rental agreements, while permanent acquisition is carried out
under the Land Acquisition Act 1894 when a well is confirmed
as producing. In such cases, compensation is determined by
the relevant state authority and awarded through the Deputy
Collector or Special Land Acquisition Officer. Landowners whose
land is acquired permanently receive fair compensation and are
considered for employment opportunities where possible.

In FY 2025-26, ONGC introduced several internal changes
to improve vendor experience. The Central Procurement
Department was reorganized into a single unified procurement
function responsible for managing high value and frequently
sourced goods and services. The Shared Finance Services
team was also assigned the role of handling centralized vendor
payments after invoice approval. This system supports consistent
service standards, improves processing timelines, and reduces
payment related issues.

registration on ONGC portals, enabling smoother participation in procurement processes.
Through these focused engagement efforts, ONGC continues to foster transparency, inclusivity, and capacity building within its
vendor base particularly encouraging participation from MSEs, including those led by women and SC/ST entrepreneurs.

Customer Centricity and Product Stewardship
ONGC remains focused on delivering consistent value and building
long term trust with its diverse customer base, which mainly
includes B2B industrial clients across crude oil, natural gas, and
related product segments. To ensure safe and reliable use of its
products, the Company follows strict national safety norms along
with global best practices. For crude oil and natural gas operations,
procedures are guided by OISD and PNGRB standards. Safety
manuals, regular drills, and regulatory audits are carried out to
protect stakeholders and maintain uninterrupted operations.
For value added products such as LPG, ATF, HSD, and naphtha,
ONGC provides Material Safety Data Sheets that outline hazard
details, safe handling practices, and emergency response
measures. This helps customers manage storage, usage, and
transport in a safe manner.

84

Integrated Report

Although ONGC operates under a bulk supply model where
standard labelling is not required, it goes beyond compliance by
installing clear signage and safety boards across pipelines and
delivery points to share product information and emergency
guidelines.
In case of any service issue or safety concern, ONGC follows a
proactive communication approach and informs customers
through formal channels to enable quick response and maintain
continuity. Customer feedback is an important part of the
Company’s improvement process and is managed through
structured systems. Feedback for crude oil is addressed through
Industry Working Group and Onshore Crude Coordination
Meetings, while gas related inputs are handled at the unit level.
For value added products, platforms such as ILP, FMDP, and IPR
are used to support ongoing engagement with customers.

Section 5: Governance
Governance Philosophy and Framework
Governance at ONGC is anchored in its long-standing institutional
legacy and its evolving mandate within India’s energy sector. As a
Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise under the Ministry of
Petroleum and Natural Gas, Government of India, the Company
approaches governance as a value-creating discipline that goes

Board of Directors and Key Managerial Personnel underwent
trainings in FY 2025-26
Transition of the Corporate Social Responsibility Committee
into the Corporate Social Responsibility & ESG Committee
Board Diversity and Experience
ONGC maintains a Board composition that reflects a balanced
mix of professional expertise, diverse perspectives, and sectorspecific experience aligned with the scale and complexity of
its operations. The Board comprises members with domain
expertise across engineering, finance, geology, legal, and human
resources, enabling informed and holistic decision-making.
Several Directors bring prior leadership experience within ONGC
and other public sector enterprises, strengthening institutional
continuity and deepening industry insight.

At ONGC, risk management is embedded as an ongoing,
enterprise-wide function that informs both operational execution
and strategic decision-making. The Company has established a
robust, multi-layered Risk Management Framework to enable
proactive identification, assessment, and mitigation of risks
across its value chain. Oversight of this framework is vested
with the Board-level Risk Management Committee, while
implementation is driven by the Risk Steering Committee and the
Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) Cell, ensuring a structured,
integrated, and responsive approach to risk governance.
Aligned with ISO 31000:2018, ONGC’s ERM framework
incorporates global best practices and adopts a dual approach:
top-down and bottom-up to capture risks comprehensively. While
the top-down approach focuses on enterprise-level risks with the
potential to impact Organizational performance, the bottom-up
approach facilitates detailed risk identification at functional and
departmental levels, ensuring timely and coordinated responses.

Training, Awareness and Skill Development at Board Level

The risk management process is systematic, beginning with
identification of risks and their potential consequences, followed
by detailed analysis of causes, triggers, likelihood, and impact.
Risks are then evaluated against defined thresholds to guide
prioritization and the selection of appropriate mitigation strategies.
ONGC also places strong emphasis on business continuity and
resilience. Comprehensive contingency frameworks, including
disaster recovery, emergency response, and crisis management
protocols are in place to address a wide spectrum of potential
disruptions, ranging from natural disasters to cyber risks.

Training and continuous learning remain integral to ONGC’s
governance philosophy, extending to the Board level. During
FY 2025–26, 100% of the Board of Directors participated in
structured training and awareness programs covering key areas
such as health and safety, ethical conduct, corporate governance,
whistleblower frameworks, regulatory compliance, and crossfunctional collaboration.

As part of its commitment to ethical governance, the Company
actively monitors and manages potential conflicts of interest at the
Board level to ensure objectivity in decision-making. Continuous
capability building through structured training and development
programs further strengthens the effectiveness of the Board
and senior leadership. Regular performance evaluations of the
highest governance body reinforce accountability and oversight.

In addition, Board members enhanced their perspectives through
participation in reputed external forums. This ongoing focus on
capability building ensures that the Board remains well-equipped
to navigate emerging risks and guide the Organization in a
complex and evolving energy landscape.

In addition, ONGC undertakes periodic corruption risk
assessments and ensures that any incidents are addressed
promptly in line with established policies. The Company maintains
transparency in disclosures and upholds strict compliance with
applicable laws and regulations across its operations, reflecting
its commitment to responsible and ethical business conduct.

Within the framework of Government-prescribed appointment
processes, ONGC continues to engage with relevant authorities
to further broaden Board diversity in a calibrated manner. This
approach supports the Company’s commitment to inclusive
governance while ensuring alignment with statutory norms and
sectoral requirements.

As a key participant in the oil and gas sector, ONGC actively

political contributions or participate in party-based funding.

supported by a robust committee structure and well-defined
policies that together ensure regulatory compliance, ethical
conduct, and effective risk management. This integrated
governance architecture enables ONGC to deliver sustained
stakeholder value while navigating the complexities of a dynamic
and evolving energy landscape.

Sustainable Governance at ONGC
ONGC has established a comprehensive sustainability governance
framework that embeds Environmental, Social, and Governance
(ESG) considerations into its strategic and operational decisionmaking processes. Anchored at the Board level and supported
by dedicated committees and internal functions, the framework
ensures effective oversight, execution, and transparent disclosure
of ESG priorities.
At the core of this approach is a multi-tiered governance
structure. The Board of Directors provides overall direction
and accountability for sustainability performance, while the
Corporate Social Responsibility Committee oversees the
planning, implementation, and impact of CSR initiatives, ensuring
alignment with national development priorities. The Risk
Management Committee integrates ESG-related risks, including
climate and reputational risks, into ERM framework, aligned with
ISO 31000:2018 and global practices. Operational responsibility
for sustainability is supported by the Carbon Management &
Sustainability Group (CM&SG), which serves as a coordinating
function for sustainability-related initiatives and facilitates the
consolidation and reporting of ESG-related information across
the Organization. The Corporate HSE and CSR functions work in
close coordination with CM&SG to implement initiatives related
to environmental stewardship, employee safety, and community
development.
Together, this governance architecture enables ONGC to adopt
a proactive, performance-oriented approach to sustainability,

ensuring that ESG considerations are closely integrated with
long-term value creation and Organizational resilience.
Strengthening Oversight: Board-Level ESG Intervention Going
Forward
As ONGC continues to align its operations with evolving global
sustainability expectations, it is strengthening Board-level
oversight of ESG matters through the proposed transformation of
its Corporate Social Responsibility & ESG (CSR&ESG) Committee.
This restructuring reflects the Company’s expanded focus
on sustainability and enhances the Board’s ability to guide
ESG strategy, monitor performance, and align decisions with
stakeholder expectations. The CSR&ESG Committee will assume
a broader mandate, integrating sustainability considerations
more closely with governance processes, including climaterelated risks, capital allocation, and long-term value creation.
Chaired by an Independent Director and comprising a balanced
mix of Independent and Whole-time Directors, the reconstituted
Committee adopts an integrated governance approach rather
than establishing a separate ESG committee. This enables ONGC
to build on existing structures while aligning with national and
global best practices.
Through this strengthened governance mechanism, ONGC aims
to deepen strategic engagement on sustainability priorities
and support its transition towards a low-carbon, inclusive, and
resilient energy future.

Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL)

On behalf of the Board of Directors of your Company, it is my
pleasure to present the 33rd Annual Report of Oil And Natural
Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC/ the Company) and its Audited
Financial Statements for the year ended 31st March, 2026
(FY’26), together with the Auditors’ Report and Comments on
the Financial Statements by the Comptroller and Auditor General
(CAG) of India.

3.

Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL)

4.

Petronet MHB Limited (PMHBL)

5.

ONGC Green Limited (OGL)

6.

ONGC Petro additions Limited (OPaL)

The global energy landscape in 2026 has entered into a phase of
heightened geopolitical uncertainty and structural transformation.
Escalating geopolitical tensions, disruptions in global energy
supply chains, and evolving trade dynamics have reinforced the
importance of energy security and resilient supply systems.
While these developments have increased market volatility, they
have also accelerated investments in technology, operational
efficiency, digitalization, and portfolio optimization across the
energy sector.
The energy transition continues to gather momentum alongside
the growing need for reliable and affordable hydrocarbons. In
this evolving environment, success depends on strategic agility,
disciplined capital allocation, technological innovation, and timely
execution. Your Company has remained focused on creating
long-term stakeholder value by strengthening its exploration and
production portfolio, sustaining capital investments, enhancing
operational efficiencies, advancing digital transformation, and
pursuing sustainable growth. These efforts position the Company
to effectively support India’s expanding energy requirements
while delivering consistent value to its stakeholders.

Major Highlights of FY’26

i.

Revenue from operations in FY’26 stood at ` 1,325,081
million against ` 1,378,463 million in FY’25.

ii.

Net profit in FY’26 was ` 328,940 million against ` 356,103
million during FY’25.

iii.

Your Company has notified 3 new hydrocarbon discoveries
(2 New Prospects viz, Vajramani & MBS191HCA-1 and 1 New
Pool discovery MBS202HAA-1) in its operated acreages.
These discoveries highlight the untapped potential of
established basins and emphasize the importance of
sustained exploration.

Your Company, along with its group companies, has registered
another year of robust performance and made substantial
progress on most of the priority areas.
Highlights of production during FY’26 are as under:
•

Crude oil production, including share of JV production, was
20.501 Million Metric Tonnes (MMT) during FY’26 against
20.892 MMT during FY’25

iv.

03 discoveries namely Gojalia-14 & Chitabari-1 in AAFB,
Tripura and Anor-1 in Cambay Basin, Gujarat were
monetized.

•

Natural gas production, including share of JV production,
was at 19.966 Billion Cubic Metres (BCM) during FY’26
against 20.190 BCM during FY’25

v.

•

Value Added Products (VAPs) production during FY’26 was
2.561 MMT against 2.596 MMT during FY’25

To improve oil and gas production from its Mumbai High
field, ONGC has collaborated with bp Exploration (Alpha) as
a Technical Services Provider (TSP) with enhanced recovery
expertise. ONGC has placed NOA (Notice of Award) for
ONGC-BP redevelopment Phase-1 Scheme on 26.12.2025.
This collaboration is designed to leverage bp’s global
expertise in managing mature reservoirs and deploying
advanced recovery technologies. This project is envisaged to
cumulative incremental production of 2.699 MMT of Oil and
2.806 BCM of Natural gas by March 2040.

vi.

ONGC has recently developed additional gas reserves of Tapti
Daman Block in Western Offshore under cluster development
concept through the Daman Upside Development Project
(DUDP). Gas production has commenced from the project in
March’2026.

Backed by an intensive and continuous exploration programme,
your Company is continuously making efforts to expand
its exploration acreages in Indian sedimentary basins and
has acquired highest OALP acreages till OALP bid round
IX. Furthermore, ONGC is evaluating the blocks on offer for
participation in ongoing OALP X & XI bid rounds.

vii.

ONGC has monetized one DSF block Chinnewala in

viii. Production Operations Control Centre (NETRA): The
Production Operation Control Centre (POCC) facility, named
NETRA, has started functioning at IPEOT, Panvel. The
Production Operation Control Centre is envisioned as ONGC’s
centralized hub for real-time monitoring, surveillance,
and optimization of production operations across its fields
and assets pan-India. It will integrate well engineering
data, real-time production data, historical data, models,
optimization workflows, and digital twin technologies into
a unified operations platform, enabling connected and
intelligent production management across ONGC.
ix.

After commencement of commercial gas production and
sales from the Bokaro CBM block in the previous year, gas
sales from North Karanpura block also started on 16th May
2025 by adopting ‘Gas ready for cascades’ model.

x.

During the year, your Company has made significant efforts
to explore the potential of unconventional reservoirs.
Eight (8) exploratory wells were drilled for Basement
exploration, including East Lakhibari-7 & Kasomarigaon-14
in Assam Shelf, MBS182HAA-2 & BH-98 in Mumbai
offshore, Padra-275, Padra-277, Padra-278 & Padra-279 in
Cambay Basin.

xi.

xii.

During the year, a total 100 conventional exploratory wells
(including 29 wells in PELs-29%) were drilled. Out of 100
exploratory wells, testing of 66 wells was concluded and 34
wells were under testing or to be tested. Out of these, 29
wells proved to be hydrocarbon bearing. Besides testing of
37 wells drilled during previous years were concluded out of
which 26 wells proved to be hydrocarbon bearing.
Success ratio in exploratory drilling achieved considering
total wells tested/concluded including those of previous
year’s wells was 1: 1.87 (53.4%) - (Total 103 wells concluded
out of which 55 wells were proved to be hydrocarbon bearing).

data was acquired during FY’26. Out of this quantum, a total
of 556.9 LKM 2D and 4016.47 SKM of 3D seismic data were
acquired in Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) blocks.

has already finalized to double its drilling efforts in next 2
years igniting India’s deepwater future under “Samudra
Manthan”.

Drilling of Wells
Your Company drilled 501 wells during FY’26 against 578
wells drilled during FY’25. 100 of these wells were exploratory
wells, while the remaining 401 wells were development wells
including side-track wells. The major highlights of Drilling
operations during the year were as under:
•

Out of the 147 wells drilled by Drilling Services
Ahmedabad, 34 wells were completed with commercial
speed exceeding 5000 M/RM

•

The first successful horizontal well in the KG Basin,
MDFT_H, targeting Mandapeta Sand-2, was drilled and
completed by rig EV-2000-1

•

Jorhat completed 14 wells (9 dev+ 5 exp)- Highest
ever in a year for Jorhat with Zero accidents (minor or
major) for FY’26

•

Drilling services, Agartala successfully utilized CNG
cascade units from Tripura Natural Gas Corporation
Limited (TNGCL) for the 1st time for commissioning
of DGB at Rig: NG-2000-1, thereby reducing HSD
consumption and carbon footprint

•

Drilling Services Frontier Basins drilled one exploratory
well each in the unexplored frontier basins of India viz.
Narmada, South Rewa & Ganga basins contributing to
assessment of new hydrocarbon prospects

•

Drilling Services (Shallow water) achieved early
monetization of two exploratory wells BH#AE and
SB#P from platform locations NK and BF, respectively,
contributing an incremental production gain of 1,700
BOPD

•

Drilling Services (Shallow water) successfully drilled
and completed three wells (B12_24P#2, B12_24P#3 &
B12_24P#4Z) on the B12_24P platform under Daman
Upside Development Project (DUDP). B12_24P#2, the
first well to be put on production, delivering ~150,000
m³/day of gas

•

Jack-up rig Deployment at Highest Water Depth
– Rig Jindal Supreme: Successfully deployed at
MBS191HCA-A open location in a water depth of 100
m, marking the deepest jack-up rig deployment along
the Indian coast

•

Statutory & Class Certifications: Secured 5-year fullterm Class and Statutory certifications for the rigs:
Sagar Ratna, Sagar Uday and Sagar Shakti

EOR Proposals
Your Company has been consistently expanding its Enhanced
Oil Recovery (EOR) portfolio. Under the Enhanced Recovery
(ER) policy, fields of ONGC located in onshore and offshore
areas were considered for screening. 33 ER Pilot/Preliminary
Screening reports for Oil Fields had been submitted to the
Directorate General Hydrocarbons (DGH) up to 31st March
2026. Out of these proposals, 17 ER Pilot schemes have
been approved (Phase-I), 3 commercial schemes were not
approved, 11 schemes are Under Approval (Phase-II) and 2
schemes have been notified to DGH.

11. Production from Overseas Assets-ONGC Videsh Ltd.

d.

High pressure- High Temperature (HP-HT) and Tight
reservoirs have been an exploration and development
challenge for your Company. Your Company is striving
hard in the field of HP-HT due to bore hole complications,
fluid design, high-cost drilling technology including
HP-HT cementing, well construction and other
reservoir engineering issues. In ONGC operated areas,
HP-HT regime is encountered in areas like Periyakudi,
Bhuvanagiri in Cauvery Onland, Kottalanka, Nagayalanka,
Bantumilli South and Malleswaram in KG Onland. Yanam
in KG Shallow offshore, G-4-6, D-33 and GS-OSN-2004/1 in
Western Offshore were also classified as HP-HT reservoirs.
Additionally, high pressure regime is often encountered in
certain areas of Assam Arakan Fold Belt. During FY’26, 4
HP/HT wells viz. Billakurru-2, Tamarada-1 & Nadipudi-1
in KG onshore and MBSWO171EAB-1 in Western Offshore
have been drilled. Billakurru-2 & MBSWO171EAB-1 were
abandoned. Tamarada-1 initially flowed gas with traces
of condensate. Nadipudi -1 was under testing as on
01.04.2026.

Your Company’s overseas E&P operations are carried out
through its wholly owned subsidiary, ONGC Videsh Limited
(OVL), which conducts its operations either directly or
through its subsidiaries. Production from the overseas
assets during FY’26 was 9.671 MMTOE in comparison
to 10.278 MMTOE during FY’25, This aggregate volume
comprised 6.908 MMT of Crude oil and 2.763 Billion Cubic
Meters (BCM) (with 1 BCM of gas equivalent to 1 MMTOE)
of Natural gas, representing an average daily production of
approximately 1,86,634 barrels of O+OEG. Despite ongoing
geopolitical challenges, the Company surpassed the 220
MMTOE cumulative production milestone, reaching a
historical total of 224.32 MMTOE as of 31st March, 2026.
The fiscal year highlighted growth trajectories across
several key assets. MECL delivered strong performance with
enhanced oil production, driving a 17% year-on-year (YoY)
increase. The asset demonstrated significant medium-term
compounding, with production surging 51% over a two-year
period and 70% over three years. Additionally, aggregate
natural gas production from the Imperial Energy, ACG, BC10, CPO-5, and A1/A3 projects grew by 4% YoY, reflecting a
7% expansion over a two-year horizon.

Moving towards digitalization using emerging technologies
